If you mean any kind of AI other than hallucinatory genAI, there is potential for AI use in work. The thing is, AI can't replace a job. It can only replace _tasks._ The elevator operator title was retired, because its definitive task (operating the elevator) was automated. The rest of what an elevator operator did moved into positions like concierge and doorman: a personable touch of welcoming, able to answer almost any building-related question, the font of information about repairs or renovations, and (if you're lucky) as the one person who sees everyone else almost daily and whose job is to pay attention to those comings and goings, a great source of gossip. All things they did as elevator operators. Really, automation didn't replace the entire job, even if the title changed. All it did was make one task obsolete. The rest of that job remained.

I believe it's too early to tell. To me it seems that AI (LLM) wasn't mainly built to make our life better (e.g. it doing the mundane things so we have more time for fun things) but specifically to save companies money by needing less employees, i.e. taking people's jobs. Further, just because the elevator operator was the only job that vanished, it doesn't also mean that other jobs didn't also suffer but maybe only still exist in some very rare niche cases. Talking about pilots, by the way, flight engineers are pretty much gone due to computers. One also has to consider the quality of the jobs technology creates. If it reduces higher level jobs, but increases low wage jobs, I'm not sure if that's a positive. I don't have much of a problem with AI privately being used to make a pyramid (although I'd prefer to learn the skill myself if possible), but nowadays you see e.g. comercial spots etc. completely in AI, and while they are off-putting and make me want to rather avoid the product, that's still a graphic designer / editor that wasn't paid or a job they could do, and I'm sure there are many other examples as well. Maybe such a job won't disappear from the list, but it could very well get reduced in numbers. This may save the company money (if the AI result isn't too off-putting), but often results in less quality. Many things today already degraded in quality, not just physical appliances, but services, too, and AI might make it even worse with the laziness that's attached to it. Problems with plagiarism are there as well, because nothing is newly created but everything is simply copied. Adding in environmental issues, problems with biases and people's cognitive abilities, I'd rather avoid AI as much as possible, and I don't see how it's a net positive, also considering all the money and ressources the AI companies are burning through... In the end, "someone using AI is taking your job" is simply semantics, and still AI taking jobs. Well, as you said, you're biased, and so were your statistics (e.g. bank teller data only up to 2010).
